pos: v. (to restore what is broken or decayed; rendering Hebrew chazaq, banah, Greek anoikodomeo)
etymology: From Latin reparo, to make ready again. Scripture's repairs are of altars, walls, and houses of God — and the man who does them is given one of the most honourable titles in the prophets.
biblical_def: To repair is to restore what has fallen into ruin, and Scripture treats the work as honourable rather than merely remedial. Isaiah gives the repairer a name: “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isaiah 58:12). The title is conferred in a chapter about true fasting, so that repairing is presented as the fruit of real religion rather than as a substitute for it. Kings are commended for the same instinct toward the house of God: “it came to pass after this, that Joash was minded to repair the house of the LORD” (2 Chronicles 24:4). The mindedness comes first and the masonry follows. The most charged repair in Scripture is Elijah's on Carmel, performed in front of a nation that had abandoned the altar it belonged to: “And Elijah said unto all the people, Come near unto me. And all the people came near unto him. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down” (1 Kings 18:30). Before fire fell, an old altar was rebuilt. Nehemiah supplies the working principle for every such labour, and it is not chiefly technique: “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6).
webster_summary: To restore to a sound state what is decayed, dilapidated or injured; to mend; to make good again. Scripture honours the repairer of the breach, records kings minded to repair God's house, and sets Elijah repairing a broken altar before fire fell.
webster_full: REPAIR, v.t. [L. reparo; re and paro, to prepare.] To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, dilapidation or partial destruction; as, to repair a house or a wall.
2. To rebuild a part decayed or destroyed; to make amends by an equivalent.
3. To fill up again; to restore; as, to repair a loss or waste.
REPAIR, v.i. To go to; to betake oneself; to resort; as, to repair to a city.
REPAIR, n. Restoration to a sound state; supply of loss; reparation; also, state as regards repairing.
REPAIRER, n. One who repairs, restores or makes amends.
scriptures: Isaiah 58:12

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
2 Chronicles 24:4
And it came to pass after this, that Joash was minded to repair the house of the LORD.
1 Kings 18:30
And Elijah said unto all the people, Come near unto me. And all the people came near unto him. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down.
Nehemiah 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.
corruption_summary: Repair has fallen out of favour as a category: what is broken is replaced, rebranded, or abandoned, and a church in decay is more readily left for a new one than mended by the men who belong to it.
corruption_paragraphs: Elijah's act on Carmel is easy to read past. Before the contest, before the fire, he repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down — an old altar, on an old foundation, in the pattern God had given. He did not erect a novel one better suited to the moment. Reformation in Scripture consistently takes that shape: not the invention of something unprecedented, but the rebuilding of what was there and had been let fall. Where a generation assumes that faithfulness requires starting fresh, it loses the very thing Isaiah 58:12 promises to honour, since a breach can only be repaired by someone willing to work on a wall he did not build.

The opposite error treats repair as a matter of masonry alone. Joash was minded to repair the house of the LORD, and Nehemiah's wall rose because the people had a mind to work; in both cases the disposition is named as the cause. Buildings, budgets, and programmes can be restored while the thing they exist to house is neglected, and Joash's own later history is the warning — the man who repaired the temple ended by forsaking the God whose house it was. Repair that stops at the fabric is not what the prophet was commending.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq (to strengthen, to repair) is the recurring verb of Nehemiah's wall; banah (to build) and rapha (to heal, mend) fill out the field, with Greek anoikodomeo (to build again) in the New Testament.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen, to repair; the verb repeated through Nehemiah 3 of each man repairing his portion.
Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build; used of building the old waste places in Isaiah 58:12.
Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to mend; used of Elijah repairing the broken altar in 1 Kings 18:30.
Hebrew perets (H6556) — a breach, a gap; the thing the honoured repairer closes.
Greek anoikodomeo (G456) — to build again, to rebuild; used of raising up the fallen tabernacle of David in Acts 15.
usage: “The repairer of the breach” — mending a wall one did not build is given an honourable name.
“He repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down” — reformation rebuilds the old pattern.
“The people had a mind to work” — the disposition is named as the cause of the building.

pos: v. (to relate or declare; also to number or count; rendering Hebrew caphar, nagad, Greek lego, eipon)
etymology: From Saxon tellan, to count or relate — the same root as tally. The older English keeps both senses, and Scripture uses them together: God tells the number of the stars, and His people tell what He has done.
biblical_def: Tell in the Authorized Version carries two senses that modern English has separated: to relate, and to count. The counting sense appears where God's knowledge is measured against man's: “He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names” (Psalm 147:4). The stars are not merely counted but named, and the psalm sets this beside His healing of the broken in heart. The same verb turns painful in the psalm of the cross, where the sufferer counts his own bones: “I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me” (Psalm 22:17). The relating sense is where duty lies. Our Lord commissions the healed man to a domestic testimony rather than a public ministry: “Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee” (Mark 5:19). And He makes telling the first step of church discipline, restricted deliberately to two people: “if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother” (Matthew 18:15). The object of that telling is stated plainly — not vindication, but a brother gained.
webster_summary: To utter; to relate; to make known; also, to number or count. Scripture has God telling the number of the stars, the sufferer telling his bones, the healed man telling his friends what the Lord has done, and a wronged brother telling a fault alone.
webster_full: TELL, v.t. [Sax. tellan, to count, to relate.] To utter; to express in words; to communicate to others; as, tell me the story.
2. To relate; to narrate; to rehearse particularly; as, to tell a tale.
3. To make known; to publish; to disclose; as, tell not this abroad.
4. To number; to count; to reckon; as, to tell money; the shepherd tells his sheep.
5. To inform; to give notice or intelligence to; as, tell him of his danger.
TELL, v.i. To give an account; to make report; also, to take effect; as, every blow tells.
scriptures: Psalm 147:4
He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.
Psalm 22:17
I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me.
Mark 5:19
Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
Matthew 18:15
Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
corruption_summary: Telling a brother his fault alone has been abandoned at both ends — either nothing is said at all, in the name of tolerance, or it is said to everyone but him, which Scripture calls talebearing rather than telling.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 18:15 prescribes a sequence that scarcely survives anywhere. The first step is private, restricted to two people, and aimed at gaining a brother rather than establishing a case. Modern practice departs in two directions at once. Some hold that saying anything at all is judgmental, and the fault goes unaddressed until it hardens; others say it freely to third parties, in confidence, as a prayer request, or online, which Scripture names as talebearing and whispering and treats among the sins that separate chief friends. Both are failures of the same command, and both leave the brother precisely where he was.

The counting sense carries its own corrective, and it is worth holding beside the other. Psalm 147:4 places God's telling of the stars in the middle of a psalm about His care for the broken in heart, so that the same knowledge which numbers and names the host of heaven is engaged with the wounds of particular people. That is the ground on which Mark 5:19 sends a delivered man home to his friends. The testimony required of him was not eloquence or scale but an account of what the Lord had done for him — a form of telling available to every believer and neglected in favour of forms that are not.
roots_summary: Hebrew caphar (to count, to recount) holds both senses in one root; nagad (to declare, to make known) supplies the relating sense; Greek lego and eipon render the ordinary telling of the New Testament.
roots_lines: Hebrew caphar (H5608) — to count, to number, to recount; the root joining telling stars and telling news.
Hebrew nagad (H5046) — to declare, to make known, to tell; used of declaring God's works among the people.
Hebrew manah (H4487) — to number, to appoint; the counting verb behind numbering days and portions.
Greek lego (G3004) — to say, to speak, to tell; the ordinary verb of the Gospels.
Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, to reprove; the verb rendered “tell him his fault” in Matthew 18:15.
usage: “He telleth the number of the stars” — the counting God also heals the broken in heart.
“Tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee” — testimony begins at home.
“Tell him his fault between thee and him alone” — the aim is a brother gained.

pos: v. (to bend or lean toward; to dispose; rendering Hebrew natah, Greek klino)
etymology: From Latin inclino, to lean or bend. Scripture uses the word for the ear that bends to listen and the heart that leans toward what it loves — and it asks God to do the inclining of the heart.
biblical_def: To incline is to lean or bend toward something, and Scripture applies it to the ear and to the heart. Of the ear it is a command, and the posture is one of deliberate attention: “So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding” (Proverbs 2:2). Wisdom is not overheard; a man must lean toward it. God Himself is said to incline His ear, and the Psalmist makes it the ground of a lifelong resolution: “Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, therefore will I call upon him as long as I live” (Psalm 116:2). Of the heart, Scripture speaks in two ways that must be held together. Joshua issues the command to a people renewing covenant: “put away… the strange gods which are among you, and incline your heart unto the LORD God of Israel” (Joshua 24:23). Yet the Psalmist knows that the heart's leaning is not finally at his own disposal, and so he prays for it: “Incline my heart unto thy testimonies, and not to covetousness” (Psalm 119:36). The command and the prayer are not rivals; the duty is real, and the ability to perform it is asked of God.
webster_summary: To lean; to bend; to deviate from a line toward an object; hence, to be disposed or favourably inclined. Scripture commands inclining the ear to wisdom and the heart to the LORD, and teaches the believer to pray that God would incline his heart.
webster_full: INCLINE, v.i. [L. inclino; in and clino, to lean.] To lean; to deviate from an erect or a horizontal line toward some object.
2. To lean; to tend; as, a man inclines to one party or opinion.
3. To be disposed; to have some wish or desire; as, I incline to go.
INCLINE, v.t. To cause to deviate from an erect or level position; to give a leaning to; as, incline the head.
2. To turn or bend toward; as, incline thine ear.
3. To give a tendency or propension to the will or affections; as, incline the heart.
scriptures: Proverbs 2:2
So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding;
Psalm 116:2
Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, therefore will I call upon him as long as I live.
Joshua 24:23
Now therefore put away, said he, the strange gods which are among you, and incline your heart unto the LORD God of Israel.
Psalm 119:36
Incline my heart unto thy testimonies, and not to covetousness.
corruption_summary: The heart's inclination is treated as a fixed and authoritative fact about a man — the thing he must follow — where Scripture treats it as the very thing that needs changing and asks God to change it.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning counsel of the age is to follow the heart, and it rests on an assumption Scripture denies: that the heart's leaning is reliable, self-authenticating, and not itself in need of correction. Psalm 119:36 assumes the opposite so completely that it makes the heart's inclination a matter for petition, and it names the rival direction explicitly — covetousness. A heart left to lean where it will does not stay neutral; it leans toward gain. To pray this verse is to concede that one's own affections are the problem rather than the compass, which is precisely the concession the surrounding culture forbids.

The opposite error uses the same verse to excuse passivity, as though a man could do nothing until God inclined him. Joshua 24:23 will not allow it. Facing a people who had strange gods among them, he commands both the putting away and the inclining, and the assembly answers with a vow. Scripture consistently commands what only God can give and gives what it commands, and the believer's part is neither self-reliance nor inertia but the ordinary means — inclining the ear to wisdom, putting away idols, and praying for a heart bent the right way.
roots_summary: Hebrew natah (to stretch out, bend, incline) covers both the ear inclined and the heart bent; Greek klino (to bend, to lean) supplies the New Testament sense.
roots_lines: Hebrew natah (H5186) — to stretch out, to bend, to incline; used of inclining the ear and of bending the heart.
Hebrew 'ozen (H241) — the ear; the member inclined in attentive hearing.
Hebrew lebab (H3824) — the heart, the inner man; the seat of the inclination Joshua commands and the Psalmist begs.
Hebrew betsa' (H1215) — covetousness, unjust gain; the rival direction named in Psalm 119:36.
Greek klino (G2827) — to bend, to incline; used of the day declining and of our Lord bowing His head.
usage: “Incline thine ear unto wisdom” — wisdom is not overheard; a man leans toward it.
“He hath inclined his ear unto me” — God's attention is the ground of lifelong prayer.
“Incline my heart unto thy testimonies” — the heart's leaning is asked of God, not followed as a guide.

pos: v. (to be cautious; to guard against; rendering Hebrew shamar, Greek blepo, prosecho)
etymology: From be and ware (wary) — literally, be wary. In Scripture the word is nearly always followed by a named danger, because biblical caution is specific rather than a general nervousness.
biblical_def: Beware is a command to wariness, and Scripture never issues it in the abstract; a particular danger is always named. Our Lord names counterfeit teachers and describes their disguise: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Matthew 7:15). The warning would be pointless if the wolves looked like wolves. He names an inward danger with equal directness and supplies the reason: “Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luke 12:15). Moses names the danger peculiar to prosperity, which is not want but forgetting: “Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage” (Deuteronomy 6:12). The warning stands in a passage about full houses and vineyards a man did not plant. Paul names an intellectual danger and marks how it works — by capture rather than persuasion: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Colossians 2:8).
webster_summary: To be cautious; to take care; to guard against danger. Scripture always attaches a named danger — false prophets, covetousness, forgetting the LORD in prosperity, and philosophy that spoils men after the tradition of men and not after Christ.
webster_full: BEWARE, v.i. [be and ware, wary.] To be cautious; to take care; to be on one's guard against danger; to be circumspect.
2. To have a care of; to guard against; followed by of; as, beware of the dog.
WARE, a. Being in expectation of; provided against; cautious; wary. [Now chiefly in beware and aware.]
WARY, a. Cautious of danger; carefully watching and guarding against deception and evils of every kind.
WARILY, adv. Cautiously; with timely caution; with prudent care to foresee and guard against evil.
WARINESS, n. Prudent care to foresee and guard against evil; cautiousness.
scriptures: Matthew 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Luke 12:15
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
Deuteronomy 6:12
Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.
Colossians 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: Warning has been reclassified as a failure of charity, so that naming false teachers is thought less Christian than tolerating them — though our Lord issued exactly such warnings and named the disguise.
corruption_paragraphs: The command to beware presupposes that some teachers are dangerous and that hearers can and must identify them. Our Lord's own warning turns on disguise: the false prophets come in sheep's clothing, which means they will look like the genuine article and will be received as such by anyone who declines to examine. A church that treats all warning as divisiveness has disarmed itself precisely where the danger is greatest, since a wolf that could be recognized without discernment would need no warning. The fruits test our Lord gives in the next verses is the appointed method, and it requires the willingness to reach a verdict.

Deuteronomy 6:12 identifies the danger the comfortable never expect. Moses warns a people about to receive houses full of good things, wells they did not dig, and vineyards they did not plant, and the peril he names is forgetting. Adversity drives men to God; abundance quietly persuades them that they need Him less, and the persuasion is not felt as apostasy at the time. Colossians 2:8 adds the third front, warning that men are spoiled — carried off as plunder — through philosophy after the tradition of men. The test Paul supplies is the only one that finally sorts it: after Christ, or not after Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamar (to keep, guard, take heed) is the standing Old Testament verb of watchful caution; Greek blepo (to look, to see to it) and prosecho (to give heed) carry the New Testament warnings.
roots_lines: Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, to guard, to take heed to oneself; the verb of Deuteronomy 6:12.
Hebrew shakach (H7911) — to forget; the specific danger warned against in a season of plenty.
Greek blepo (G991) — to see, to look to, to beware; the imperative of Colossians 2:8.
Greek prosecho (G4337) — to hold to, to give heed, to beware of; used of taking heed to false prophets.
Greek sulagogeo (G4812) — to carry off as spoil; Paul's vivid word for what philosophy does to the unwary.
usage: “Beware of false prophets… in sheep's clothing” — the warning assumes a convincing disguise.
“Beware lest thou forget the LORD” — the danger of plenty is forgetting, not want.
“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy” — the test is after Christ, or not.

pos: v. (to make greater in size or room; to set at liberty; rendering Hebrew rachab, Greek platuno)
etymology: From en and large. The Hebrew behind it means to make broad, and Scripture uses it for a widened tent, a widened path under the feet, a widened heart, and a man given room when he was in distress.
biblical_def: To enlarge is to make room, and Scripture uses it for deliverance as often as for increase. Under pressure the Psalmist reports it as an act of God upon a confined man: “Thou hast enlarged my steps under me, that my feet did not slip” (Psalm 18:36). Broad footing rather than a narrow ledge is what keeps a man upright. Isaiah issues it as a command to a barren woman who is told to prepare for children she does not yet have: “Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” (Isaiah 54:2). Faith enlarges before the increase arrives, and the command to strengthen the stakes belongs with it, since a wider tent needs deeper anchorage. Jabez prays for enlargement of territory and is granted it, though the prayer is bounded on either side by the presence of God's hand and preservation from evil: “Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil” (1 Chronicles 4:10). Paul uses the word for affection rather than acreage: “O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6:11).
webster_summary: To make greater in quantity, extent or room; to expand; to set at liberty. Scripture uses it of steps enlarged so the feet do not slip, of a tent widened in faith, of Jabez's coast, and of an apostle's heart enlarged toward a difficult church.
webster_full: ENLARGE, v.t. [en and large.] To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits, breadth or size; as, to enlarge a house or a field.
2. To expand; to dilate; to make more comprehensive; as, to enlarge the heart or the understanding.
3. To increase in appearance; to magnify to the eye.
4. To set free; to release from confinement or oppression; as, to enlarge a prisoner.
ENLARGE, v.i. To grow large or larger; to extend; to dilate; also, to expatiate; to speak or write at length upon a subject.
ENLARGEMENT, n. Increase of size or bulk; expansion; also, release from confinement or servitude.
scriptures: Psalm 18:36
Thou hast enlarged my steps under me, that my feet did not slip.
Isaiah 54:2
Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes;
1 Chronicles 4:10

And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.
2 Corinthians 6:11
O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged.
corruption_summary: The prayer of Jabez has been detached from its book and its terms and marketed as a technique for personal expansion, with the request for God's hand and for keeping from evil quietly dropped from the middle of it.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Chronicles 4:10 sits in the middle of nine chapters of genealogy, and the whole point of its placement is that God noticed one man in a list. The popular treatment reverses this, extracting the verse as a formula for enlargement and promising that repetition will produce increase. Two of the four petitions are usually neglected: that God's hand might be with him, and that he might be kept from evil so that it would not grieve him. A prayer for a wider coast without those two is a prayer for more territory than a man can hold without harm, and Scripture's own histories are full of kings whose borders grew and whose souls did not.

Isaiah 54:2 supplies the corrective picture. The command to enlarge the tent is given to the barren, before any children appear, and it comes paired with a second command — strengthen thy stakes. Enlargement without anchorage produces a structure that the first wind takes down, which is exactly what happens to ministries expanded faster than they are founded. Paul's use in 2 Corinthians 6:11 names the enlargement most worth seeking: a heart made wide toward a congregation that had wounded him. That kind of increase costs the man who receives it and injures nobody.
roots_summary: Hebrew rachab (to be or grow wide, to make room) supplies every Old Testament instance; Greek platuno (to make broad) renders the enlarged heart of 2 Corinthians 6:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew rachab (H7337) — to be wide, to enlarge, to make room; the verb of enlarged steps and an enlarged coast.
Hebrew merchab (H4800) — a broad place, room, liberty; the large place into which the LORD brings the delivered.
Hebrew gebuwl (H1366) — border, coast, territory; the thing Jabez asked to have enlarged.
Greek platuno (G4115) — to make broad, to enlarge; used of the enlarged heart and of broadened phylacteries.
Greek stenochoreo (G4729) — to be straitened, cramped; the opposite condition Paul names in the next verse.
usage: “Thou hast enlarged my steps under me” — room to stand is itself a deliverance.
“Enlarge the place of thy tent… strengthen thy stakes” — widening and anchoring are commanded together.
“Our heart is enlarged” — the enlargement most worth seeking is of the affections.

pos: adj. (moving with speed; quick; rendering Hebrew qal, mahar, Greek tachus)
etymology: From Saxon swift, quick. Scripture never treats speed as a virtue in itself: it commands swiftness in hearing, denies that the race is to the swift, and warns that God Himself will be a swift witness.
biblical_def: Swift means quick in motion, and Scripture assigns the quality with care. It is commanded in exactly one direction, and deliberately balanced against two slownesses: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath” (James 1:19). The ordering is the point. Where speed governs speech and temper instead of hearing, the proportions are simply reversed. Speed is also denied its usual advantage: “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise… but time and chance happeneth to them all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11). The Preacher is not denying that swiftness helps in a race; he is denying that the swift may count on the outcome, which providence governs. Amos presses the same denial into judgment, where the fastest man discovers that speed will not carry him out: “Therefore the flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not strengthen his force, neither shall the mighty deliver himself” (Amos 2:14). And Malachi puts the adjective where it is most sobering, on God as witness: “I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless” (Malachi 3:5).
webster_summary: Moving with great speed or velocity; fleet; rapid; ready. Scripture commands men to be swift to hear and slow to speak, denies that the race is to the swift, and warns that the LORD will be a swift witness against particular sins.
webster_full: SWIFT, a. [Sax. swift.] Moving a great distance or over a large space in a short time; moving with celerity or velocity; fleet; rapid; quick; speedy.
2. Ready; prompt; as, swift to hear.
3. Of short continuance; passing quickly; as, swift destruction.
SWIFT, n. The current of a stream; also, a bird of the swallow kind, remarkable for its rapid flight.
SWIFTLY, adv. With celerity or velocity; fleetly; rapidly; with quick motion.
SWIFTNESS, n. Speed; rapid motion; quickness; celerity; velocity; rapidity.
scriptures: James 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Ecclesiastes 9:11

I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
Amos 2:14
Therefore the flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not strengthen his force, neither shall the mighty deliver himself:
Malachi 3:5

And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: James's proportions have been inverted by an age built for instant reply: men are swift to speak and swift to wrath, and the one swiftness commanded — hearing — is the one now least practised.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:19 reads as a direct description of modern discourse with every term reversed. The instruments men now use for speech are designed for immediate response and reward the quickest and most heated reply, which means the ordinary conditions of life train the two slownesses out of a man while making speed of speech and of anger effortless. The verse is not a counsel of passivity. Swiftness is commanded — toward hearing — and hearing in James means the receiving of the engrafted word and the doing of it. A generation swift in the two forbidden directions and slow in the commanded one has exactly inverted the Apostle's order.

The second corruption is confidence in speed itself, and Ecclesiastes 9:11 addresses it without cynicism. The Preacher grants that swiftness, strength, wisdom, and skill are real advantages; he denies that they secure the result, because time and chance — which the believer knows as providence — happen to them all. That is a rebuke to the man who trusts his own quickness and a comfort to the man who has none. Malachi 3:5 completes the picture by putting the adjective where it belongs at last: the LORD is the swift one, and He is swift as a witness against the very oppressions that fast and clever men commit.
roots_summary: Hebrew qal (light, swift) and mahar (to hasten) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek tachus (quick, swift) is the adjective of James 1:19.
roots_lines: Hebrew qal (H7031) — light, swift; used of swift runners and of the swift of foot in Amos 2:14.
Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, to be swift; the verb behind the LORD's swift witness in Malachi 3:5.
Hebrew merowts (H4793) — a running, a race; the race that is not to the swift in Ecclesiastes 9:11.
Greek tachus (G5036) — quick, swift, ready; the adjective governing “swift to hear”.
Greek bradus (G1021) — slow, dull; the counterpart commanded toward speech and wrath.
usage: “Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath” — speed is commanded in one direction only.
“The race is not to the swift” — advantage is real; the outcome is providence's.
“I will be a swift witness” — the swiftness that finally matters is God's.

pos: v. (to lay out or consume; to pass, as time; rendering Hebrew kalah, shaqal, Greek dapanao)
etymology: From Latin expendo, to weigh out. What is spent is weighed out and gone, and Scripture asks of every expenditure — of money, of days, of a life — what was bought with it.
biblical_def: To spend is to lay out what one has, and Scripture presses the question of what is bought. Isaiah puts it to a people spending on the wrong things: “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness” (Isaiah 55:2). The rebuke is not against spending but against the purchase: money laid out for what is not bread, labour for what does not satisfy. Days are spent as surely as coin, and Moses measures them without flattery: “For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told” (Psalm 90:9). A whole life goes the way a story goes — told, and over. Job describes the prosperous who spend well by every visible measure and arrive nowhere: “They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave” (Job 21:13). And the prodigal's ruin is dated precisely from the moment his spending ended: “And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want” (Luke 15:14). The famine was already coming; the spending merely removed his cushion against it.
webster_summary: To lay out; to dispose of; to part with; to consume; to pass, as time. Scripture asks what a man's money and days purchase, warns of spending for what is not bread, and dates the prodigal's want from the moment he had spent all.
webster_full: SPEND, v.t. [L. expendo, to weigh out.] To lay out; to dispose of; to part with; as, to spend money for clothing.
2. To consume; to waste; to squander; as, to spend an estate in gaming.
3. To bestow for any purpose; to employ; as, to spend one's labor or pains.
4. To pass, as time; to suffer to pass away; as, to spend a day or a year.
5. To exhaust of force or strength; as, a spent ball; the storm is spent.
SPEND, v.i. To make expense; to lay out or consume money or other property; also, to be consumed or wasted.
scriptures: Isaiah 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
Psalm 90:9
For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told.
They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave.
Luke 15:14
And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.
corruption_summary: Spending is now audited only for value received in this life, so Isaiah's question — why lay out money for what is not bread — is answered by better shopping rather than by a different appetite.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 55:2 asks a question that sounds financial and is not. The prophet is addressing men who are getting exactly what they paid for and remain unfed, and his remedy is not thrift but a different table: hearken diligently, eat that which is good, let your soul delight itself in fatness. Where the question is heard as counsel about budgeting, it is answered by spending more wisely on the same class of goods, and the soul goes on unsatisfied at a better price. The corruption is not extravagance; it is the assumption that satisfaction is purchasable at all, which the whole chapter exists to deny.

Psalm 90:9 and Job 21:13 press the same audit on time, which is the one currency no man can stop spending. Moses does not say our years are stolen or wasted; he says they are spent, laid out as a tale is told, and he draws from it the prayer to be taught to number our days. Job's prosperous men spend theirs in wealth and go down in a moment. The prodigal's case joins both threads: he spent all, and the famine that was coming anyway found him with nothing. Scripture's counsel is not to spend less but to know what is being bought, since the expenditure continues whether it is examined or not.
roots_summary: Hebrew kalah (to finish, to consume) and shaqal (to weigh out money) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek dapanao (to spend, to consume) governs the prodigal's account.
roots_lines: Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to complete, to consume, to spend; used of years spent and strength consumed.
Hebrew shaqal (H8254) — to weigh out; the verb behind “spend money” in Isaiah 55:2, money being weighed silver.
Hebrew hegeh (H1899) — a moaning, a tale, a meditation; the “tale that is told” of Psalm 90:9.
Greek dapanao (G1159) — to spend, to consume, to squander; the prodigal's verb in Luke 15:14.
Greek ekdapanao (G1550) — to spend utterly, to exhaust; Paul's word for being spent for the souls of others.
usage: “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” — the question is about appetite, not budgeting.
“We spend our years as a tale that is told” — time is laid out whether or not it is counted.
“When he had spent all… he began to be in want” — the famine was already coming.

pos: n. & v. (a reckoning to be rendered; to reckon or impute; rendering Hebrew chashab, Greek logos, logizomai)
etymology: From Old French aconter, to reckon or count. Scripture uses the counting-house word for the two greatest reckonings: what God imputes to the believer, and what every man must render at the last.
biblical_def: Account is a reckoning, and Scripture uses the word for both the ledger God keeps and the entry He makes. The reckoning to be rendered is universal and personal: “So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God” (Romans 14:12). Not of others, and not by proxy — of himself. Our Lord extends the audit to the smallest item of speech: “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). Idle words are precisely the ones no man records, which is why the reckoning must be God's. A particular accountability rests on those who lead, and the writer to the Hebrews makes the congregation's obedience a mercy to their own pastors: “Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief” (Hebrews 13:17). Against that whole weight stands the other use, in which God credits a man with what he does not possess: “Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness” (Galatians 3:6). Faith is not the payment; it is the empty hand to which righteousness is reckoned.
webster_summary: A reckoning or computation; a statement of debts and credits; also, to reckon, to esteem, to impute. Scripture teaches that every man shall give account of himself to God, that rulers watch as those who must give account, and that righteousness was accounted to Abraham on believing.
webster_full: ACCOUNT, n. [Fr. conte, a reckoning.] A sum stated on paper; a registry of a debt or credit; of debts and credits, or charges.
2. A computation of debts and credits, or a general statement of particular sums; as, the account stands thus.
3. A reckoning; a rendering of reasons; as, he must give account of his conduct.
4. Value; importance; estimation; as, a man of no account.
ACCOUNT, v.t. To deem, judge, consider, think or hold in opinion; as, I account him a worthy man.
2. To reckon or compute; to assign or impute; as, it was accounted to him for righteousness.
scriptures: Romans 14:12
So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.
Matthew 12:36
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
Hebrews 13:17

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
Galatians 3:6
Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.
corruption_summary: Final accountability has been dissolved — either into a general assurance that nothing will be asked, or into a merely horizontal accountability to peers — while the imputation that answers it is treated as a legal fiction rather than God's own reckoning.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 14:12 says three things the age resists: there will be an account, it will be given to God, and it will be given of oneself. Popular religion softens each in turn, assuming that no reckoning will be required, that any reckoning is to a vaguely benevolent principle rather than to a Person, and that responsibility can be distributed across systems and circumstances until no individual holds it. Matthew 12:36 blocks the last exit by naming idle words — items too small to be anyone's policy and impossible to blame on structures. What is trivial enough to be forgotten by the speaker is still on the ledger.

The answering corruption dismisses imputation as an accounting trick, on the ground that calling a sinner righteous does not make him so. Galatians 3:6 uses the counting-house verb deliberately, and the Reformed doctrine follows the text rather than softening it: righteousness is accounted, credited to the believer's account on the ground of Christ's obedience and death, received by faith and not produced by it. That is not a fiction, because the reckoning is God's own and He is the one whose ledger stands. Hebrews 13:17 then shows the doctrine working downward into ordinary church life, where a congregation may make its watchmen's account a joy or a grief.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab (to reckon, impute, esteem) is the verb of Genesis 15:6 behind Galatians 3:6; Greek logos (a word, a reckoning) and logizomai (to reckon, to impute) supply the New Testament senses.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, to reckon, to impute; the verb of righteousness counted to Abraham.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to number, to call to account; used of God visiting iniquity and mustering a people.
Greek logos (G3056) — a word, an account, a reckoning; the noun in “give account” at Romans 14:12.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to count, to impute; the verb of Galatians 3:6 and Romans 4.
Greek ellogeo (G1677) — to charge to one's account; Paul's word to Philemon, offering to have Onesimus' debt put on his.
usage: “Every one of us shall give account of himself to God” — the reckoning is personal and unavoidable.
“Every idle word… they shall give account thereof” — the smallest items are on the ledger.
“It was accounted to him for righteousness” — God's own reckoning credits what faith receives.

pos: n. (a castrated man, often a court officer; rendering Hebrew cariyc, Greek eunouchos)
etymology: From Greek eunouchos, keeper of the bed — a trusted officer of a royal household. The Hebrew word covers both the physically emasculated and, more broadly, court officials of high trust.
biblical_def: A eunuch in Scripture is a man made incapable of offspring, commonly an officer of a royal court; the Hebrew word extends to trusted officials generally. Under the law such a man was excluded from the congregation (Deuteronomy 23:1), and Isaiah addresses the grief that exclusion produced: “neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree” (Isaiah 56:3). The complaint is that he has no future, since in Israel a man's future was his children. The answer is one of the most striking promises in the prophets: “Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off” (Isaiah 56:5). What he cannot obtain by descent God gives directly, and gives better. The book of Acts records the promise beginning to be kept when the gospel goes to a court official of Ethiopia: “a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship” (Acts 8:27). Our Lord also uses the term for those who forgo marriage for the kingdom's sake: “there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it” (Matthew 19:12).
webster_summary: A male of the human species castrated, and often employed as a keeper or officer in eastern courts. Scripture records the eunuch's exclusion under the law, Isaiah's promise of a name better than sons and daughters, and the Ethiopian officer's baptism.
webster_full: EUNUCH, n. [Gr. eunouchos; eune, a bed, and echo, to keep.] A male of the human species castrated; and hence, in eastern countries, an officer entrusted with the care of the women's apartments.
2. In a general sense, an officer of a court or household of high trust.
EUNUCH, v.t. To make a eunuch; to castrate. [Rarely used.]
EUNUCHATE, v.t. To make a eunuch; to deprive of the power of generation.
CHAMBERLAIN, n. An officer charged with the direction and management of a chamber or chambers; in the East, frequently a eunuch.
COURTIER, n. One who attends or frequents the courts of princes.
scriptures: Isaiah 56:3
Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people: neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree.
Isaiah 56:5
Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off.
Acts 8:27

And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship,
Matthew 19:12

For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother's womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 56 and Matthew 19 are now regularly enlisted to bless what Scripture treats as a loss God graciously compensates — and to imply that the body's created form is negotiable, which neither passage teaches.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 56 is a text of comfort, and its comfort depends on an honest reading of the situation. The eunuch calls himself a dry tree, and the prophet does not tell him he is mistaken about his condition; he tells him God will give him something better than sons and daughters. That is compensation for a real loss, not a revaluation of it as no loss at all. Where the passage is used to suggest that Scripture is indifferent to the body's created integrity, the argument runs against the chapter's own logic, since a promise to a dry tree presupposes that a dry tree is a grief. God's tenderness toward such men — and it is remarkable tenderness, given the law's exclusion — is tenderness precisely in the face of a genuine deprivation.

Matthew 19:12 is similarly pressed beyond its sense. Our Lord names three cases, and the third — those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake — has always been understood by the church, against Origen's literal self-mutilation, as the voluntary forgoing of marriage for undivided service, which Paul commends in 1 Corinthians 7 without commanding it. The saying is bounded on both sides: it is given in a discussion of marriage and divorce, and it closes with “He that is able to receive it, let him receive it” — a gift for some, never a general rule, and never a warrant for treating the body given by the Creator as raw material.
roots_summary: Hebrew cariyc (a eunuch; also a court official) covers both senses; Greek eunouchos (keeper of the bed) names the office, and dunastes (a man of authority) describes the Ethiopian's rank.
roots_lines: Hebrew cariyc (H5631) — a eunuch; also, more broadly, a court officer or chamberlain of trust.
Hebrew yad (H3027) — hand, and by extension a place or monument; the “place” promised within God's walls in Isaiah 56:5.
Hebrew shem (H8034) — a name; the everlasting name given in place of sons and daughters.
Greek eunouchos (G2135) — a eunuch, a keeper of the bed; the word of Matthew 19:12 and Acts 8.
Greek dunastes (G1413) — a potentate, a man of great authority; the Ethiopian's standing in Acts 8:27.
usage: “Neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree” — the grief is real and is answered, not denied.
“A name better than of sons and of daughters” — God gives directly what descent could not supply.
“He that is able to receive it, let him receive it” — the saying is a gift for some, not a rule for all.

pos: adj. (crippled or disabled in a limb; rendering Hebrew picceach, Greek cholos)
etymology: From Saxon lama, weak or crippled. Scripture uses lameness for the disqualified offering, for the man carried to a king's table by mercy, and for the healing that will mark the age to come.
biblical_def: Lame describes disability in the feet or legs, and Scripture puts the word to three distinct uses. In sacrifice it marks what may not be offered, and the prophet exposes the contempt behind such gifts by a simple test: “if ye offer the lame and sick, is it not evil? offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee, or accept thy person? saith the LORD of hosts” (Malachi 1:8). What no man would present to a magistrate was being presented to God. In narrative, lameness is the setting for kindness that costs the giver and cannot be repaid: Mephibosheth, the last of a fallen house, “did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet” (2 Samuel 9:13). The clause about his feet is placed last, after his seat at the table, which is where the emphasis belongs. In prophecy, lameness is what the coming kingdom undoes: “Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert” (Isaiah 35:6). And in exhortation, the writer to the Hebrews makes the lame the measure of how a congregation should walk: “make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed” (Hebrews 12:13).
webster_summary: Crippled or disabled in a limb, or otherwise injured so as to be unsound; halt. Scripture forbids the lame as an offering, seats lame Mephibosheth at the king's table, promises the lame shall leap as an hart, and commands straight paths for the sake of the lame.
webster_full: LAME, a. [Sax. lama, weak, crippled.] Crippled or disabled in a limb, or otherwise injured so as to be unsound and impaired in strength; as, a lame arm or leg.
2. Hobbling; not smooth; as, a lame gait.
3. Imperfect; not satisfactory; as, a lame excuse.
LAME, v.t. To make lame; to cripple or disable; to render imperfect and unsound.
LAMELY, adv. Like a cripple; in a halting manner; imperfectly; weakly; poorly.
LAMENESS, n. An impaired state of the body or limbs; loss of natural soundness; imperfection; weakness.
scriptures: Malachi 1:8

And if ye offer the blind for sacrifice, is it not evil? and if ye offer the lame and sick, is it not evil? offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee, or accept thy person? saith the LORD of hosts.
2 Samuel 9:13
So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem: for he did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet.
Isaiah 35:6
Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert.
Hebrews 12:13
And make straight paths for your feet, lest that which is lame be turned out of the way; but let it rather be healed.
corruption_summary: The offering standard of Malachi 1 has been quietly abandoned in worship, while the pastoral standard of Hebrews 12 — ordering the church's walk so the lame are not turned out of the way — is neglected in favour of the strong.
corruption_paragraphs: Malachi's test is uncomfortably practical: offer it to your governor and see whether he accepts it. The lame animal cost the worshipper nothing, since it was worth little and would soon be worth less, and that is exactly what made the gift an insult. The principle is not confined to livestock. Where the leftovers of a week — unprepared preaching, unconsidered giving, attention already spent elsewhere — are brought to God on the assumption that He is less discriminating than a magistrate, the prophet's question stands unanswered. The remedy is not scrupulosity about ritual but the recovery of the plain thought that God is worth a man's best.

Hebrews 12:13 turns the same word toward the congregation and produces a duty the strong rarely feel. The paths a church walks — its pace, its expectations, the assumptions built into its common life — are to be made straight so that the lame are not turned out of the way but healed. That is an argument from the weakest member rather than the strongest, and it cuts against every instinct to organize around those who can keep up. Mephibosheth is the picture of the outcome: a man with nothing to offer and no means of repayment, seated continually at the king's table for the sake of a covenant made with another.
roots_summary: Hebrew picceach (lame) marks both the disqualified offering and the man shown kindness; Greek cholos (lame, halt) carries the New Testament healings and the exhortation of Hebrews 12:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew picceach (H6455) — lame; used of the offering that may not be brought and of Mephibosheth.
Hebrew nakeh (H5223) — smitten, stricken, contrite; the term joined to lameness in Mephibosheth's account.
Hebrew 'ayyalah (H355) — a hind, a hart; the leaping creature the healed lame man is compared to in Isaiah 35:6.
Greek cholos (G5560) — lame, halt, maimed; the word of Hebrews 12:13 and of the lame healed at the Beautiful gate.
Greek iaomai (G2390) — to heal, to cure; the outcome commanded for the lame rather than their turning aside.
usage: “Offer it now unto thy governor” — the test exposes what a cheap offering says about the receiver.
“Did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet” — the seat comes before the disability.
“Lest that which is lame be turned out of the way” — the church's pace is set by its weakest.
